\hypertarget{def:column-hilbert-corner}{}%
\begin{definition}[level-one and amplified column-Hilbert corner\normalfont{} (\texttt{def-\allowbreak{}column-\allowbreak{}hilbert-\allowbreak{}corner})]\label{def:column-hilbert-corner}
Let $P$ and $Q$ be $\delta$-projections in an $\varepsilon$-$C^*$ algebra. If $Q$ is one-dimensional, then $\mathcal{S}_{P,Q}$ is a Hilbert space with the inner product $\langle{\cdot},{\cdot}\rangle$ defined by the equation
\begin{equation*}
Y^\dagger\cdot X=\langle{Y},{X}\rangle\,\widetilde{Q}\qquad (X,Y\in\mathcal{S}_{P,Q}),
\end{equation*}
where $Y^\dagger\cdot X=\mathrm{C}_{Q}(Y^{\dagger}X)$ and $\widetilde{Q}=\mathrm{C}_Q(Q)$.

\noindent\textbf{One-dimensional projections and the corresponding Hilbert spaces.} Lemma~\textup{[\texttt{lem\_PQ\_Hilb}]} says that if $P,Q\in\mathcal{A}$ are $\delta$-projections and $Q$ is one-dimensional, then the space $\mathcal{S}_{P,Q}$ is equipped with the Hermitian inner product given by \textup{[\texttt{1dQ\_ip}]}. The extended version of this space, $\mathbb{C}^n\otimes\mathcal{S}_{P,Q}=\mathbf{M}_{n,1}\otimes\mathcal{S}_{P,Q}$, satisfies essentially the same equation:
\begin{equation*}
Y^\dagger\cdot X=\langle{Y},{X}\rangle\,\widetilde{Q}\qquad (X,Y\in\mathbf{M}_{n,1}\otimes\mathcal{S}_{P,Q}),
\end{equation*}
where $\langle{Y},{X}\rangle=\sum_{l}\langle{[Y]_{l1}},{[X]_{l1}}\rangle$.
\end{definition}

\defsourceline{\begin{Lemma}\label{lem_PQ_Hilb}}
\defsourceline{Let $P$ and $Q$ be $\delta$-projections in an $\eps$-$C^*$ algebra. If $Q$ is one-dimensional, then $\calS_{P,Q}$ is a Hilbert space with the inner product $\braket{\cdot}{\cdot}$ defined by the equation}
\defsourceline{\begin{equation}\label{1dQ_ip}}
\defsourceline{Y^\dag\cdot X=\braket{Y}{X}\,\wt{Q}\qquad (X,Y\in\calS_{P,Q}),}
\defsourceline{\end{equation}}
\defsourceline{where $Y^\dag\cdot X=\Co_{Q}(Y^{\dag}X)$ and $\wt{Q}=\Co_Q(Q)$.}
\end{defsourcequote}
\begin{defsourcequote}
\defsourceline{\noindent\textbf{One-dimensional projections and the corresponding Hilbert spaces.} Lemma~\ref{lem_PQ_Hilb} says that if $P,Q\in\calA$ are $\delta$-projections and $Q$ is one-dimensional, then the space $\calS_{P,Q}$ is equipped with the Hermitian inner product given by \eqref{1dQ_ip}. The extended version of this space, $\CC^n\otimes\calS_{P,Q}=\Ma{n,1}\otimes\calS_{P,Q}$, satisfies essentially the same equation:}
\defsourceline{\begin{equation}\label{1dQ_ip_ext}}
\defsourceline{Y^\dag\cdot X=\braket{Y}{X}\,\wt{Q}\qquad (X,Y\in\Ma{n,1}\otimes\calS_{P,Q}),}
\defsourceline{\end{equation}}
\defsourceline{where $\braket{Y}{X}=\sum_{l}\braket{[Y]_{l1}}{[X]_{l1}}$.}

%% ---- def-compressed-corner ---------------------------------------------
\hypertarget{def:compressed-corner}{}%
\begin{definition}[compressed corner\normalfont{} (\texttt{def-\allowbreak{}compressed-\allowbreak{}corner})]\label{def:compressed-corner}
To each pair of projections $(P,Q)$ in a $C^*$ algebra $\mathcal{B}$, one assigns the vector space $\mathcal{S}_{P,Q}=\{PXQ:\,X\in\mathcal{B}\}$. In this section, we discuss an approximate version of this construction. Recall that a $\delta$-projection in an $\varepsilon$-$C^*$ algebra $\mathcal{A}$ is a Hermitian element $P$ such that $\|P^2-P\|\le\delta$. For each pair $(P,Q)$ of $\delta$-projections, there are two slightly different maps that could be called ``compressions'': $\mathrm{L}_P\mathrm{R}_Q\colon X\mapsto P(XQ)$ and $\mathrm{R}_Q\mathrm{L}_P\colon X\mapsto (PX)Q$. We will use their symmetric combination, $\frac{1}{2}(\mathrm{L}_P\mathrm{R}_Q+\mathrm{R}_Q\mathrm{L}_P)$. It is an $O(\delta+\varepsilon)$-idempotent element of the algebra of operators acting on $\mathcal{A}$, and therefore, can be approximated by an idempotent using Proposition~\textup{[\texttt{prop\_P}]}. The \emph{compression map} thus defined,
\begin{equation*}
\mathrm{C}_{P,Q}\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A},\qquad
\mathrm{C}_{P,Q}=\theta(\mathrm{L}_P\mathrm{R}_Q+\mathrm{R}_Q\mathrm{L}_P-1),
\end{equation*}
satisfies the equations
\begin{equation*}
\mathrm{C}_{P,Q}^2=\mathrm{C}_{P,Q},\qquad\:
\mathrm{C}_{P,Q}(X)^\dagger=\mathrm{C}_{Q,P}(X^\dagger)\quad\: (X\in\mathcal{A}),
\end{equation*}
and both $\|\mathrm{L}_P\mathrm{R}_Q-\mathrm{C}_{P,Q}\|$ and $\|\mathrm{R}_Q\mathrm{L}_P-\mathrm{C}_{P,Q}\|$ are bounded by $O(\delta+\varepsilon)$. The image of this map, $\mathcal{S}_{P,Q}=\operatorname{Im}\mathrm{C}_{P,Q}=\operatorname{Ker}(1-\mathrm{C}_{P,Q})$, is a closed linear subspace of $\mathcal{A}$. There is a variant of this construction where only $\mathrm{L}_P$ or only $\mathrm{R}_Q$ is applied, and one writes $\mathrm{C}_{P,1},\mathcal{S}_{P,1}$ or $\mathrm{C}_{1,Q},\mathcal{S}_{1,Q}$, respectively. (This is the same as $\mathrm{C}_{P,I}$, etc.\ if the unit is exact.)

When $P=Q$, the abbreviations $\mathrm{C}_{P}$, $\mathcal{S}_P$ are used.

For any triple $(P,Q,R)$ of $\delta$-projections, one defines the \emph{compressed product} between elements of the corresponding subspaces:
\begin{equation*}
(X,Y)\mapsto X\cdot Y\,\colon\,
\mathcal{S}_{P,Q}\times\mathcal{S}_{Q,R}\to \mathcal{S}_{P,R},\qquad X\cdot Y=\mathrm{C}_{P,R}(XY).
\end{equation*}
It is close to the ambient product in $\mathcal{A}$, namely, $\|X\cdot Y-XY\|\le O(\delta+\varepsilon)\|X\|\mkern1mu\|Y\|$. If $P$ is a nonvanishing projection, the compressed product turns the Banach space $\mathcal{S}_P$ (which is closed under the involution $X\mapsto X^\dagger$) into an $O(\delta+\varepsilon)$-$C^*$ algebra with unit $\widetilde{P}=\mathrm{C}_{P}(P)$.\medskip
\end{definition}

%% ---- def-delta-projection ----------------------------------------------
\hypertarget{def:delta-projection}{}%
\begin{definition}[$\delta$-projection and nonvanishing alternative\normalfont{} (\texttt{def-\allowbreak{}delta-\allowbreak{}projection})]\label{def:delta-projection}
A \emph{projection} in an $\varepsilon$-$C^*$ algebra $\mathcal{A}$ is a Hermitian element $P$ such that $P^2=P$. Such elements are generally hard to come by, see Remark~\textup{[\texttt{rem\_X2}]}, so will content ourselves with \emph{$\delta$-projections} for sufficiently small $\delta$. They are defined by the conditions
\begin{equation*}
P^\dagger=P,\qquad \|P^2-P\|\le\delta.
\end{equation*}

\begin{equation*}
\|P\|\le O(\delta)\quad \text{or}\quad \bigl|\|P\|-1\bigr|\le O(\delta+\varepsilon).
\end{equation*}
A $\delta$-projection is called \emph{nonvanishing} if the second alternative holds. If $P$ is a $\delta$-projection, then $I-P$ is a $\delta'$-projection, where $\delta'=\delta$ if $\mathcal{A}$ has exact unit and $\delta'=\delta+O(\varepsilon)$ in general. A $\delta$-projection $P$ is called \emph{nontrivial} if both $P$ and $I-P$ are nonvanishing.
\end{definition}

%% ---- def-epsilon-cstar-algebra -----------------------------------------
\hypertarget{def:epsilon-cstar-algebra}{}%
\begin{definition}[$\varepsilon$-$C^{*}$-algebra\normalfont{} (\texttt{def-\allowbreak{}epsilon-\allowbreak{}cstar-\allowbreak{}algebra})]\label{def:epsilon-cstar-algebra}
An \emph{$\varepsilon$-Banach algebra} is a Banach space $\mathcal{A}$ endowed with a bilinear multiplication map $\mathcal{A}\times \mathcal{A}\to \mathcal{A}$ such that
\begin{alignat*}{2}
\|XY\| &\le (1+\varepsilon)\mkern1mu\|X\|\mkern1mu\|Y\|\qquad &&(X,Y\in \mathcal{A}),\\[2pt]
\|(XY)Z-X(YZ)\| &\le \varepsilon\mkern1mu\|X\|\mkern1mu\|Y\|\mkern1mu\|Z\|\qquad &&(X,Y,Z\in \mathcal{A}).
\end{alignat*}
Such an algebra is called \emph{$\varepsilon'$-commutative} if
\begin{equation*}
\|XY-YX\|\le \varepsilon'\mkern1mu\|X\|\mkern1mu\|Y\|\qquad (X,Y\in \mathcal{A}).
\end{equation*}
A \emph{$*\varepsilon$-Banach algebra} is a complex $\varepsilon$-Banach algebra with a conjugate linear involution $X\mapsto X^\dagger$ satisfying the equations
\begin{equation*}
\|X^\dagger\|=\|X\|,\qquad (XY)^\dagger=Y^\dagger X^\dagger\qquad (X,Y\in \mathcal{A}).
\end{equation*}
An \emph{$\varepsilon$-$C^*$ algebra} is one with this additional property:
\begin{equation*}
\|X^{\dagger}X\|\ge (1-\varepsilon)\mkern1mu\|X\|^{2}\qquad (X\in \mathcal{A}).
\end{equation*}
(A bound from the other side, $\|X^{\dagger}X\|\le (1+\varepsilon)\mkern1mu\|X\|^{2}$, follows from \textup{[\texttt{ax\_prodnorm}]} and \textup{[\texttt{ax\_*}]}.) We assume that all algebras are unital. The unit element $I\in\mathcal{A}$ should satisfy the approximate or exact conditions
\begin{alignat*}{4}
\|XI&-X\|\le\varepsilon\mkern1mu\|X\|,\qquad &\|IX&-X\|\le\varepsilon\mkern1mu\|X\|,\qquad
&\bigl|\|I\|&-1\bigr|\le\varepsilon\qquad &&\text{(by default)},\quad \text{or}\\[2pt]
XI&=X,\qquad &IX&=X,\qquad
&\|I\|&=1\qquad &&\text{(if specified)}.
\end{alignat*}
If the involution is defined, one also requires that $I^\dagger=I$.
\end{definition}

\textbf{Kind.} cited (byte-matched to a pinned source under \texttt{refs/}); \texttt{status: locked}.\quad\textbf{Aliases.} epsilon-$C^{*}$-algebra; approximate $C^{*}$-algebra.

\defsourcecheckhead{Source check (byte-verbatim) --- \texttt{kitaev-\allowbreak{}2405.\allowbreak{}02434,\allowbreak{} approximate\_algebras.\allowbreak{}tex:\allowbreak{}407-\allowbreak{}440}}
\begin{defsourcequote}
\defsourceline{\begin{Definition}}
\defsourceline{An \emph{$\eps$-Banach algebra} is a Banach space $\calA$ endowed with a bilinear multiplication map $\calA\times \calA\to \calA$ such that}
\defsourceline{\begin{alignat}{2}}
\defsourceline{\label{ax_prodnorm}}
\defsourceline{\|XY\| &\le (1+\eps)\ts\|X\|\ts\|Y\|\qquad &&(X,Y\in \calA),\\[2pt]}
\defsourceline{\label{ax_assoc}}
\defsourceline{\|(XY)Z-X(YZ)\| &\le \eps\ts\|X\|\ts\|Y\|\ts\|Z\|\qquad &&(X,Y,Z\in \calA).}
\defsourceline{\end{alignat}}
\defsourceline{Such an algebra is called \emph{$\eps'$-commutative} if}
\defsourceline{\begin{equation}}
\defsourceline{\label{ax_comm}}
\defsourceline{\|XY-YX\|\le \eps'\ts\|X\|\ts\|Y\|\qquad (X,Y\in \calA).}
\defsourceline{\end{equation}}
\defsourceline{A \emph{$*\eps$-Banach algebra} is a complex $\eps$-Banach algebra with a conjugate linear involution $X\mapsto X^\dag$ satisfying the equations}
\defsourceline{\begin{equation}}
\defsourceline{\label{ax_*}}
\defsourceline{\|X^\dag\|=\|X\|,\qquad (XY)^\dag=Y^\dag X^\dag\qquad (X,Y\in \calA).}
\defsourceline{\end{equation}}
\defsourceline{An \emph{$\eps$-$C^*$ algebra} is one with this additional property:}
\defsourceline{\begin{equation}}
\defsourceline{\label{ax_C*}}
\defsourceline{\|X^{\dag}X\|\ge (1-\eps)\ts\|X\|^{2}\qquad (X\in \calA).}
\defsourceline{\end{equation}}
\defsourceline{(A bound from the other side, $\|X^{\dag}X\|\le (1+\eps)\ts\|X\|^{2}$, follows from \eqref{ax_prodnorm} and \eqref{ax_*}.) We assume that all algebras are unital. The unit element $I\in\calA$ should satisfy the approximate or exact conditions}
\defsourceline{\begin{alignat}{4}}
\defsourceline{\label{ax_eps_unit}}
\defsourceline{\|XI&-X\|\le\eps\ts\|X\|,\qquad &\|IX&-X\|\le\eps\ts\|X\|,\qquad}
\defsourceline{&\bigl|\|I\|&-1\bigr|\le\eps\qquad &&\text{(by default)},\quad \text{or}\\[2pt]}
\defsourceline{\label{ax_exact_unit}}
\defsourceline{XI&=X,\qquad &IX&=X,\qquad}
\defsourceline{&\|I\|&=1\qquad &&\text{(if specified)}.}
\defsourceline{\end{alignat}}
\defsourceline{If the involution is defined, one also requires that $I^\dag=I$.}
\defsourceline{\end{Definition}}
\end{defsourcequote}

%% ---- def-extended-epsilon-cstar-algebra --------------------------------
\hypertarget{def:extended-epsilon-cstar-algebra}{}%
\begin{definition}[extended $\varepsilon$-$C^{*}$-algebra\normalfont{} (\texttt{def-\allowbreak{}extended-\allowbreak{}epsilon-\allowbreak{}cstar-\allowbreak{}algebra})]\label{def:extended-epsilon-cstar-algebra}
An \emph{extended $\varepsilon$-$C^*$ algebra} is a complete self-adjoint operator space $\mathcal{A}$ with a multiplication and a unit that make each space $\mathbf{M}_{n}\otimes\mathcal{A}$ into an $\varepsilon$-$C^*$ algebra. An \emph{extended $\delta$-homomorphism} is a linear map $v\colon\mathcal{A}'\to\mathcal{A}''$ such that for each $n$, the map $1_{\mathbf{M}_{n}}\otimes v\colon \mathbf{M}_{n}\otimes\mathcal{A}'\to\mathbf{M}_{n}\otimes\mathcal{A}''$ is a $\delta$-homomorphism.
\end{definition}

%% ---- def-fd-cstar-diagonal ---------------------------------------------
\hypertarget{def:fd-cstar-diagonal}{}%
\begin{definition}[diagonal of a finite-dimensional $C^{*}$-algebra\normalfont{} (\texttt{def-\allowbreak{}fd-\allowbreak{}cstar-\allowbreak{}diagonal})]\label{def:fd-cstar-diagonal}
For arbitrary $\tilde{D}=\sum_{j}A_j\otimes B_j\in\mathcal{B}\otimes\mathcal{B}$ and $X\in\mathcal{B}$, we write
\begin{equation*}
X\tilde{D}=\sum_{j}XA_j\otimes B_j,\qquad
\tilde{D}X=\sum_{j}A_j\otimes B_jX,\qquad
\pi(\tilde{D})=\sum_{j}A_jB_j.
\end{equation*}
These operations extend from $\mathcal{B}\otimes\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{B}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}\mathcal{B}$. An element $D\in\mathcal{B}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}\mathcal{B}$ is called a \emph{diagonal} if
\begin{equation*}
XD=DX\quad\text{for all }\, X\in\mathcal{B},\qquad \pi(D)=I_\mathcal{B}.
\end{equation*}
\end{definition}
\begin{defnote}
\textbf{Kind.} cited (byte-matched to a pinned source under \texttt{refs/}); \texttt{status: locked}.\quad\textbf{Aliases.} finite-dimensional $C^{*}$-algebra diagonal; algebra diagonal.
\par

\par

%% ---- def-h-space-left-inversion ----------------------------------------
\hypertarget{def:h-space-left-inversion}{}%
\begin{definition}[H-space and left inversion\normalfont{} (\texttt{def-\allowbreak{}h-\allowbreak{}space-\allowbreak{}left-\allowbreak{}inversion})]\label{def:h-space-left-inversion}
An \emph{H-space} is a topological space $M$ with basepoint
$e$ and a continuous multiplication $\mu\colon M\times M\to M$ with $\mu(e,e)=e$
such that $x\mapsto\mu(x,e)$ and $x\mapsto\mu(e,x)$ are each basepoint-preserving
homotopic to the identity. It is \emph{associative} if the two triple-product maps are
homotopic. An \emph{inversion map} is a continuous basepoint-preserving
$\sigma\colon M\to M$ with both $x\mapsto\mu(\sigma(x),x)$ and
$x\mapsto\mu(x,\sigma(x))$ homotopic to the constant map $e$; when only the first
homotopy is required, $\sigma$ is a \emph{left inversion map}.
\end{definition}
\begin{defnote}
\textbf{Kind.} cited (byte-matched to a pinned source under \texttt{refs/}); \texttt{status: locked}.\quad\textbf{Aliases.} H-space; associative H-space; inversion map; left inversion map.
\par
\textbf{Provenance.} \texttt{source: kitaev-\allowbreak{}2405.\allowbreak{}02434}; locus \texttt{approximate\_algebras.\allowbreak{}tex:\allowbreak{}895-\allowbreak{}912}; \textsc{sha256} prefix \texttt{e7eb512a2ec2438d}; record: byte-\allowbreak{}match lock per definitions/\allowbreak{}README.\allowbreak{}md (cited criterion);\allowbreak{} provisioned by DESIGN-\allowbreak{}FUDW-\allowbreak{}DECOMP-\allowbreak{}v4.\allowbreak{}1.\allowbreak{}md \S{}4.\allowbreak{}1 (kind "cited /\allowbreak{} lock after byte-\allowbreak{}match").
\par

\par

register row: ``pinned TeX 895--912, definition only'') --- no claim about $\mathcal U$
or any Stage-1 object is carried by this shard. Source typo note: the source
writes $\mu\colon M\to M$ for the multiplication map's type where

\defsourceline{\begin{equation}\label{H-unit}}
\defsourceline{\bigl(x\mapsto \mu(x,e)\bigr)}
\defsourceline{\,\sim\,\bigl(x\mapsto x\bigr)}

%% ---- def-ha-map --------------------------------------------------------
\hypertarget{def:ha-map}{}%
\begin{definition}[Ha-map\normalfont{} (\texttt{def-\allowbreak{}ha-\allowbreak{}map})]\label{def:ha-map}
Let $Q$ be a one-dimensional $\delta$-projection in an $\varepsilon$-$C^*$ algebra $\mathcal{A}$. For any $\delta$-projections $P,R\in\mathcal{A}$, we define a map $\mathrm{H}^{Q}_{P,R}\colon\mathcal{S}_{P,R}\to\mathbf{B}(\mathcal{S}_{R,Q},\mathcal{S}_{P,Q})$. (Here $\mathbf{B}(\mathcal{S}_{R,Q},\mathcal{S}_{P,Q})$ is the space of bounded linear maps from $\mathcal{S}_{R,Q}$ to $\mathcal{S}_{P,Q}$ with the norm induced by the Euclidean norm $\|X\|_\mathrm{E}=\sqrt{\langle{X},{X}\rangle}$. Due to inequality \textup{[\texttt{1dQ\_ip\_norm}]}, the latter is equal to $\|X\|$ up to a $1\pm O(\varepsilon+\delta)$ factor.) For each $Z\in\mathcal{S}_{P,R}$ and $X\in\mathcal{S}_{R,Q}$, the element $\mathrm{H}^{Q}_{P,R}(Z)(X)\in\mathcal{S}_{P,Q}$ is defined by the condition
\begin{equation*}
(Y^\dagger\cdot Z)\cdot X+Y^\dagger\cdot(Z\cdot X)
=2\,\bigl\langle{Y},\mkern1mu{\mathrm{H}^{Q}_{P,R}(Z)(X)}\bigr\rangle\,\widetilde{Q}\quad \text{for all }\,Y\in\mathcal{S}_{P,Q}.
\end{equation*}
\end{definition}
\begin{defnote}
\textbf{Kind.} cited (byte-matched to a pinned source under \texttt{refs/}); \texttt{status: locked}.\quad\textbf{Aliases.} Ha map; Kitaev Ha-map.
\par
\textbf{Provenance.} \texttt{source: kitaev-\allowbreak{}2405.\allowbreak{}02434}; locus \texttt{approximate\_algebras.\allowbreak{}tex:\allowbreak{}1146-\allowbreak{}1149}; \textsc{sha256} prefix \texttt{e7eb512a2ec2438d}.
\par

The byte-verbatim source is reproduced below as the second check.

%% ---- def-lefschetz-fixed-point-data ------------------------------------
\hypertarget{def:lefschetz-fixed-point-data}{}%
\begin{definition}[Lefschetz number and local fixed-point index\normalfont{} (\texttt{def-\allowbreak{}lefschetz-\allowbreak{}fixed-\allowbreak{}point-\allowbreak{}data})]\label{def:lefschetz-fixed-point-data}
For a smooth self-map $f$ of a compact orientable
manifold $M$: at a fixed point $x$ with $\det(1-f'(x))\ne0$ (where
$f'(x)\colon T_xM\to T_xM$ is the differential), the \emph{fixed point index} is
$\operatorname{ind}(f,x)=\operatorname{sgn}\det(1-f'(x))$; the \emph{Lefschetz number}
is $\Lambda(f)=\sum_k(-1)^k\operatorname{Tr}f^{*k}$, where
$f^{*k}\colon H^k(M;\mathbb R)\to H^k(M;\mathbb R)$ is the induced map on real
cohomology.
\end{definition}
\begin{defnote}
\textbf{Kind.} cited (byte-matched to a pinned source under \texttt{refs/}); \texttt{status: locked}.\quad\textbf{Aliases.} Lefschetz number; fixed point index; fixed-point index; ind(f,x); Lambda(f).
\par
\textbf{Provenance.} \texttt{source: kitaev-\allowbreak{}2405.\allowbreak{}02434}; locus \texttt{approximate\_algebras.\allowbreak{}tex:\allowbreak{}961-\allowbreak{}967}; \textsc{sha256} prefix \texttt{e7eb512a2ec2438d}; record: byte-\allowbreak{}match lock per definitions/\allowbreak{}README.\allowbreak{}md (cited criterion);\allowbreak{} provisioned by DESIGN-\allowbreak{}FUDW-\allowbreak{}DECOMP-\allowbreak{}v4.\allowbreak{}1.\allowbreak{}md \S{}4.\allowbreak{}1 (kind "cited /\allowbreak{} lock after byte-\allowbreak{}match").

register row: ``pinned TeX 957--967, definitions only''): this shard carries the two
displayed definitions and NO theorem content --- in particular it does not assert
the Lefschetz--Hopf identity $\sum_{x\in\operatorname{Fix}(f)}\operatorname{ind}(f,x)=\Lambda(f)$
(that is the separate result row \texttt{lem-\allowbreak{}topology-\allowbreak{}lefschetz-\allowbreak{}hopf}, to be \texttt{cited}
from Arkowitz--Brown), nor the index-sign theorem (\texttt{lem-\allowbreak{}topology-\allowbreak{}local-\allowbreak{}index-\allowbreak{}sign},
Granas--Dugundji). The source's index formula is stated in the nondegenerate
($\det\ne0$) smooth case; the general topological index the theorem rows use is

\defsourceline{The \emph{fixed point index} $\ind(f,x)$ and the \emph{Lefschetz number} $\Lambda(f)$ are defined as follows:}
\defsourceline{\begin{alignat}{2}}
\defsourceline{\ind(f,x)&=\sgn\det(1-f'(x)),\qquad}

%% ---- def-one-dimensional-delta-projection ------------------------------
\hypertarget{def:one-dimensional-delta-projection}{}%
\begin{definition}[one-dimensional $\delta$-projection and equivalence\normalfont{} (\texttt{def-\allowbreak{}one-\allowbreak{}dimensional-\allowbreak{}delta-\allowbreak{}projection})]\label{def:one-dimensional-delta-projection}
When $P=Q$, the abbreviations $\mathrm{C}_{P}$, $\mathcal{S}_P$ are used. It is clear that $\mathcal{S}_P=0$ if and only if $P$ is sufficiently close to $0$ as described by the first alternative in \textup{[\texttt{P\_alternatives}]}. (Recall that in the opposite case, we call $P$ ``nonvanishing''.) Similarly, $\mathrm{C}_P=1$ and $\mathcal{S}_P=\mathcal{A}$ if and only if $P$ is close to $I$. If $\dim\mathcal{S}_P=1$, we say that $P$ is a \emph{one-dimensional $\delta$-projection}.

One-dimensional $\delta$-projections $P$ and $Q$ are called \emph{equivalent} if $\dim\mathcal{S}_{P,Q}=1$. This is indeed an equivalence relation; in particular, it is transitive due to Lemma~\textup{[\texttt{lem\_PQR}]}.
\end{definition}
\begin{defnote}

\begin{defsourcequote}
\defsourceline{When $P=Q$, the abbreviations $\Co_{P}$, $\calS_P$ are used. It is clear that $\calS_P=0$ if and only if $P$ is sufficiently close to $0$ as described by the first alternative in \eqref{P_alternatives}. (Recall that in the opposite case, we call $P$ ``nonvanishing''.) Similarly, $\Co_P=1$ and $\calS_P=\calA$ if and only if $P$ is close to $I$. If $\dim\calS_P=1$, we say that $P$ is a \emph{one-dimensional $\delta$-projection}.}
\end{defsourcequote}
\begin{defsourcequote}
\defsourceline{One-dimensional $\delta$-projections $P$ and $Q$ are called \emph{equivalent} if $\dim\calS_{P,Q}=1$. This is indeed an equivalence relation; in particular, it is transitive due to Lemma~\ref{lem_PQR}.}
\end{defsourcequote}

%% ---- def-projection-basis ----------------------------------------------
\hypertarget{def:projection-basis}{}%
\begin{definition}[projection basis of a finite-dimensional commutative $C^{*}$-algebra\normalfont{} (\texttt{def-\allowbreak{}projection-\allowbreak{}basis})]\label{def:projection-basis}
The second application of Lemma~\textup{[\texttt{lem\_merging}]} involves an auxiliary statement about $\delta$-projections $P_1,\dots,P_p,Q_1,\dots,Q_q$ satisfying certain conditions, which will be formulated in terms of inclusions of finite-dimensional commutative $C^*$ algebras. Such an algebra $\mathcal{B}$ is described by a \emph{projection basis} $\{\Pi_1,\dots,\Pi_n\}\subseteq\mathcal{B}$ such that $\Pi_j^\dagger=\Pi_j$,\, $\Pi_j\Pi_k=\delta_{jk}\Pi_k$, and $\sum_{j=1}^{n}\Pi_j=I$.
\end{definition}

%% ---- def-theta-idempotent-approximation --------------------------------
\hypertarget{def:theta-idempotent-approximation}{}%
\begin{definition}[theta idempotent-approximation map\normalfont{} (\texttt{def-\allowbreak{}theta-\allowbreak{}idempotent-\allowbreak{}approximation})]\label{def:theta-idempotent-approximation}
Power-series functional calculus (tex:505-510):

\begin{gather*}
f(X)=a_0I+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_n(X-x_0I)^n\quad\:
\text{if }\, \|X-x_0I\|<r,\\
\|f(X)-f(x_0I)\|\le \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}|a_n|\mkern1mu\|X-x_0I\|^n.
\end{gather*}

Absolute value and sign (tex:517-520):

\begin{gather*}
|X|=(X^2)^{1/2},\qquad \operatorname{sgn}(X)=X(X^2)^{-1/2}\qquad\quad
\bigl(\|X^2-x_0^2I\|<x_0^2\bigr).
\end{gather*}

The theta map (tex:527-528, the definitional display of Proposition \texttt{prop\_P}):

\begin{gather*}
\widetilde{P}=\theta(2P-I),\qquad
\text{where}\quad \theta(X)=\frac{1}{2}\bigl(I+\operatorname{sgn}(X)\bigr).
\end{gather*}
\end{definition}
\begin{defnote}
\textbf{Kind.} cited (byte-matched to a pinned source under \texttt{refs/}); \texttt{status: draft}.\quad\textbf{Aliases.} theta map; functional-calculus idempotent approximation.
